newsitem.title: USA: Mass house rejects Weld tax cuts in its plan - paper.
newsitem.headline: Mass house rejects Weld tax cuts in its plan - paper.

text.p: The Massachusetts House plans to reject all of the seven tax cuts proposed by Gov William Weld and undercut his pledge to give legal immigrants relief from new welfare rules, the Boston Globe said Monday.
The House wishes to support Food Stamps and Medicaid coverage for legal immigrants, but not cash payments, which Weld and the state Senate have backed.

The $18.3 billion fiscal 1998 plan by the House Ways and Means Committee would spend $93 million more than Weld's budget on paying off unfunded pension liabilities, but not go along with the governor's plans for $83 million in tax cuts, including reductions for unearned income and increases in deductions for dependent children, the paper said.

The House initially had seemed more receptive to Weld's tax cuts and the chairman of the committee, Paul Heley, a Weymouth Democrat,did not rule out considering reductions later in the year, but he first wants the proposals fully studied by the Committee on Taxation.

The division between the governor's and House's plans in part reflects a difference over how to handle the rising revenues generated by an improving economy, the paper said. It added Weld appeared to be influenced in part by the race he lost last November to Sen. John Kerry, a Democrat, in which the governor was criticized for failing to adquately fund human services and pressing for tax cuts that favored the wealthy.
The House wants to use an unexpected rise in revenues to improve the state's bond rating, raise the Rainy Day fund, and complete some capital projects that were approved but not fully funded.
Haley noted that the $500 million prison bond bill approved two years ago so far has only resulted in one new prison, and had virtually no effect on overcrowding, the paper said.
